title: Primary Function
learningObjectives: Explain how the drive transmits power.
student: Explain how the motor, pulleys, and V-belt work together to transmit power to the blower.
instructor: The motor rotates the small driving pulley. Unequal tensile forces in the belt transmit torque to the larger driven pulley, which rotates the blower shaft and impeller.

title: External Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the torque and belt forces in the load path.
student: Identify the motor torque applied to the driving pulley and the tensile forces carried by the tight and slack belt spans.
instructor: The motor shaft applies torque M to the driving pulley. The belt carries a larger tight-side tensile force T1 and a smaller slack-side tensile force T2; their moment difference transmits the motor torque.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Identify the pulley axes and limits of the belt-tension model.
student: Identify the motor and blower shafts as the pulley axes. Explain why bearing reactions are outside the intended belt-tension calculation.
instructor: The motor shaft and blower shaft define the fixed pulley axes. Their bearings support the pulley force resultants, but bearing reactions are excluded because the assigned analysis is limited to torque transmission and belt tension.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace power transfer from motor to blower.
student: Trace the power and load transfer from the motor to the blower.
instructor: Power flows from the motor through the motor shaft and driving pulley, into the V-belt through unequal span tensions, into the driven pulley and blower shaft, and finally to the blower rotor.

title: Critical Belt Region
student: Identify the belt region carrying the larger tensile force.
instructor: The tight side carries T1, the larger tensile force, and is therefore the governing belt region for the assigned equivalent-area stress check.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Relate belt tension to the educational stress extension.
student: Identify the relevant tensile force and average tensile stress in the belt. Explain why the tight side is more critical than the slack side.
instructor: Each straight span carries axial tension, and the teaching extension represents its average stress as σ=T/Aeq. Because T1 is larger than T2, the tight-side average stress is larger and governs this comparison.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify inputs governing belt tension and the stress extension.
student: Identify the parameters needed to determine the belt tensions and perform the instructor-defined equivalent-area stress check.
instructor: The required inputs are motor power P, motor speed n, motor-pulley diameter D1, the specified ratio k=T2/T1, equivalent area Aeq, and allowable stress σallow.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a mechanics model of the belt drive.
student:
Create a simplified two-pulley V-belt model. Show the motor pulley, driven pulley, tight-side force T1, slack-side force T2, and motor-pulley diameter D1. Preserve the power-transmission load path without reproducing the photograph's exact geometry.

STUDENT MODEL / FREE-BODY DIAGRAM SPACE
instructor: A suitable model contains the small motor pulley and larger driven blower pulley connected by two straight belt spans. Label the motor torque, motor-pulley radius or diameter, tight-side tension T1, slack-side tension T2, and rotation direction.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions and distinguish the educational extension from commercial design.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real belt drive into the simplified model.
instructor:
• Operation is steady and the belt does not slip.
  • Belt mass and centrifugal effects are negligible.
  • The supplied ratio k=T2/T1 represents the operating tension relationship.
  • Each straight belt span carries uniform axial tension.
  • The instructor-defined Aeq is used only for an educational average-stress check.
  • Pulley and shaft stress, local belt bending, fatigue, wear, thermal effects, startup transients, and detailed V-groove contact mechanics are neglected.
  • The equivalent-area check is not a commercial V-belt sizing method.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Describe the sequence for calculating the belt tensions and completing the limited stress assessment.
instructor:
1. Convert speed to angular velocity.
  2. Compute motor torque from P=Mω.
  3. Use M=(T1−T2)r1.
  4. Combine this with T2=kT1 to solve both tensions.
  5. Verify power with P=(T1−T2)v.
  6. For the instructor-defined extension, compute σ=T/Aeq and compare the tight-side value with σallow.

title: Angular Velocity
student: Convert the motor speed n to angular velocity ω in rad/s.

title: Motor Torque
learningObjectives: Determine torque from power and speed.
student: Determine the torque M delivered by the motor using P=Mω.

title: Required Tension Difference
learningObjectives: Relate motor torque to the belt-tension difference.
student: For motor-pulley radius r1=D1/2, determine the required tension difference T1−T2 from M=(T1−T2)r1.

title: Tight-Side and Slack-Side Tensions
student: Using the specified ratio T2/T1=k, determine the tight-side tension T1 and slack-side tension T2.
instructor:
With T2=kT1, the torque equation gives T1(1−k) = {{v_belt_tension_difference_N}} N.

T1 = {{v_belt_T1_N}} N = {{v_belt_T1_kN}} kN

T2 = {{v_belt_T2_N}} N = {{v_belt_T2_kN}} kN

title: Power Verification
learningObjectives: Verify transmitted power from belt forces and speed.
instructor: v=ωr1 = {{v_belt_speed_m_s}} m/s. Therefore, P=(T1−T2)v = {{v_belt_power_check_kW}} kW, matching the assigned motor power.

title: Equivalent-Area Tensile Stress
learningObjectives: Apply average normal stress to the instructor-defined equivalent member.
student: As an instructor-defined Solid Mechanics idealization, treat the belt as an equivalent axial tensile member. Determine the average tight-side stress σ1=T1/Aeq and slack-side stress σ2=T2/Aeq.
instructor:
σ1 = ({{v_belt_T1_N}} N)/({{v_belt_A_eq_mm2}} mm2) = {{v_belt_sigma1_MPa}} MPa.

σ2 = ({{v_belt_T2_N}} N)/({{v_belt_A_eq_mm2}} mm2) = {{v_belt_sigma2_MPa}} MPa.

This is an instructor-defined equivalent-area comparison, not a standard commercial V-belt sizing calculation.

title: Allowable-Stress Assessment
learningObjectives: Compare the governing idealized stress with the assigned allowable value.
student: Compare the governing tight-side stress with the instructor-specified allowable stress. Determine σallow/σ1 and state whether the idealized equivalent-tension model passes.

title: Commercial-Selection Limitations
learningObjectives: Identify refinements required for real belt selection.
student: Explain which assumptions would need refinement for selection of a real commercial V-belt.
instructor: Commercial selection should use manufacturer power ratings and account for pulley diameters, wrap angle, service factor, belt speed, number of belts, pretension, centrifugal effects, fatigue and wear, temperature, alignment, startup loading, and V-groove contact. A reinforced composite belt is not designed by a simple gross-area allowable-stress check.

title: Limited Engineering Recommendation
learningObjectives: Make a recommendation bounded by the teaching model.
student: Make a limited recommendation: acceptable under the assigned idealized model, or requires a larger effective belt area, an additional belt, or lower transmitted power.
instructor:
{{v_belt_engineering_recommendation}}

The recommendation applies only to the instructor-defined equivalent-tension model and is not approval or selection of a commercial V-belt.
